label: conj:onepower
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj:onepower}
Every prime $p$ can be written as $p = 2^a + m$, where $a \ge 0$ is an integer and $m$ is a squarefree positive integer.
head: environment
name: Erd\H{o}s, one-power version

label: def:squarefree
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:squarefree}
A positive integer $m$ is \textit{squarefree} if no prime square divides $m$; equivalently, $m = \operatorname{rad}(m)$, where $\operatorname{rad}(m)$ denotes the product of the distinct primes dividing $m$. For a polynomial $F$, $\operatorname{rad}(F)$ denotes the product of the distinct irreducible factors of $F$.
head: environment

label: def:x
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:x}
For $p = 36k + 7$ with $k \ge 0$, define $x = 6k + 1$, so that $p = 6x + 1$. Note that $x$ is odd and $x \equiv 1 \pmod 3$; in particular $\gcd(x, 6) = 1$.
head: environment

label: lem:forms
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:forms}
Let $p = 36k+7$ and $x = 6k+1$. Then
\[
p - 1 = 6x, \qquad
p - 2 = 6x - 1, \qquad
p - 4 = 3(2x - 1), \qquad
p - 8 = 6x - 7,
\]
and more generally $p - 2^a = 6x - (2^a - 1)$ for every $a \ge 0$ with $2^a < p$. Moreover, for every prime $q \ge 5$,
\[
q^2 \mid p - 1 \text{ if and only if } q^2 \mid x,
\qquad
q^2 \mid p - 4 \text{ if and only if } q^2 \mid 2x - 1,
\]
and $p - 1$ (resp.\ $p-2$, $p-4$, $p-8$) is squarefree if and only if $x$ (resp.\ $6x-1$, $2x-1$, $6x-7$) is squarefree.
\footnote{Lean 4 formalizations of the four remainder identities, squarefree equivalences, and resulting representation criterion in Section 2.1 are available at https://github.com/shenharman/erdos-7-mod-36.}
head: environment
name: Reduction to linear forms

title: Proof
body_md: Since $p = 6x + 1$, the identity $p - 2^a = 6x - (2^a - 1)$ is immediate; the displayed cases are $a = 0, 1, 2, 3$ (for $a = 2$ note $6x - 3 = 3(2x-1)$). For the squarefree equivalences: $p - 1 = 6x = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot x$ with $\gcd(x, 6) = 1$, and $6$ is squarefree, so $p-1$ is squarefree if and only if $x$ is; the prime squares $4$ and $9$ never divide $6x$. Similarly $p - 4 = 3(2x-1)$ with $2x - 1$ odd and $2x - 1 \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, so $\gcd(3, 2x-1) = 1$ and $p - 4$ is squarefree if and only if $2x-1$ is. Finally $6x - 1$ and $6x - 7$ are odd and coprime to $3$, so their squarefreeness is unaffected by the primes $2, 3$; obstructions to any of the four forms must come from primes $q \ge 5$.
head: environment

label: def:completefailure
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:completefailure}
A prime $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$ is a \emph{complete failure} if none of $p-1$, $p-2$, $p-4$, $p-8$ is squarefree; equivalently, by Lemma~\ref{lem:forms}, if all four of $x$, $6x-1$, $2x-1$, $6x-7$ are non-squarefree at $x = (p-1)/6$.
head: environment
name: Complete failure

label: lem:excluded
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:excluded}
Let $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$ and $a \ge 0$. Then $9 \mid p - 2^a$ if and only if $a \equiv 4 \pmod 6$. In particular $p - 16 = 9(4k - 1)$ is never squarefree, and the admissible exponents are exactly those with $a \not\equiv 4 \pmod 6$. Moreover $4 \nmid p - 2^a$ for every $a$, so for admissible $a$ every prime square obstructing $p - 2^a$ satisfies $q \ge 5$.
head: environment
name: Excluded exponents

title: Proof
body_md: The order of $2$ modulo $9$ is $6$, with $2^0, \dots, 2^5 \equiv 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 5 \pmod 9$. Since $p \equiv 7 \pmod 9$, we have $9 \mid p - 2^a$ if and only if $2^a \equiv 7 \pmod 9$, that is, if and only if $a \equiv 4 \pmod 6$. Reducing $p - 2^a$ modulo $9$ for $a \equiv 0, 1, \dots, 5 \pmod 6$ gives the residues $6, 5, 3, 8, 0, 2$ respectively. Hence $3$ exactly divides $p - 2^a$ when $a \equiv 0, 2 \pmod 6$ --- in particular $3 \parallel p - 1 = 6x$, since $x \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, and $3 \parallel p - 4 = 3(2x-1)$ --- while $3 \nmid p - 2^a$ when $a \equiv 1, 3, 5 \pmod 6$. In no admissible case does $9$ divide $p - 2^a$. For the prime $2$, if $a = 0$ then $p - 1 \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, because $p - 1 = 6x$ with $x$ odd, and if $a \ge 1$ then $p - 2^a$ is odd.
head: environment

label: thm:mirsky
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Mirsky

label: thm:coprime
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Pairwise coprimality

title: Proof
body_md:
We compute each gcd by eliminating $x$.
(i) Any common divisor of $x$ and $6x - 1$ divides $6x - (6x-1) = 1$.
(ii) Any common divisor of $x$ and $2x - 1$ divides $2x - (2x-1) = 1$.
(iii) Any common divisor $d$ of $x$ and $6x - 7$ divides $6x - (6x - 7) = 7$, so $d \in \{1, 7\}$; and since $6x - 7 \equiv -x \pmod 7$, we have $7 \mid x$ if and only if $7 \mid 6x-7$.
(iv) Any common divisor of $6x-1$ and $2x-1$ divides $(6x-1) - 3(2x-1) = 2$; both quantities are odd, so the gcd is $1$.
(v) Any common divisor of $6x - 1$ and $6x - 7$ divides their difference $6$; both are odd and coprime to $3$, so the gcd is $1$.
(vi) Any common divisor of $2x-1$ and $6x-7$ divides $3(2x-1) - (6x - 7) = 4$; both are odd, so the gcd is $1$.
Finally, if $49 \mid x$ and $49 \mid 6x - 7$, then $49 \mid 6x - (6x-7) = 7$, a contradiction; so $49$ divides at most one of the pair.
head: environment

label: cor:separation
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:separation}
For every prime $q \ge 5$, the square $q^2$ divides at most one of the four quantities $x$, $6x-1$, $2x-1$, $6x-7$.
head: environment
name: Strong separation

title: Proof
body_md: If $q \ne 7$, then by Theorem~\ref{thm:coprime} the prime $q$ itself divides at most one of the four quantities, so a fortiori $q^2$ does. If $q = 7$, the only pair with a possible common factor is $(x, 6x-7)$, and the final assertion of Theorem~\ref{thm:coprime} shows $49$ divides at most one of them.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The size estimate used above --- that two of the four remainders differ by at most $7$, while $q^2 \ge 25$ --- is the whole of the argument, and it requires nothing of $p$ beyond $q \ge 5$. The same estimate reappears in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:sf}, where it is what makes non-coprime tuples of moduli vanish. Lemma~\ref{lem:primaryfailure} is then the special case in which the obstructed form is $x$ itself.
head: environment

label: lem:primaryfailure
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:primaryfailure}
Let $x = 6k+1$ and let $q \ge 5$ be prime with $q^2 \mid x$. Then $q^2 
mid 6x - 1$, $q^2 
mid 2x - 1$, and $q^2 
mid 6x - 7$.
head: environment
name: Primary Failure Lemma

title: Proof
body_md: If $q^2 \mid x$ then modulo $q^2$ we have $6x - 1 \equiv -1$, $2x - 1 \equiv -1$, and $6x - 7 \equiv -7$. Since $q \ge 5$, the modulus $q^2 \ge 25$ divides none of $1, 1, 7$.
head: environment
name: First proof (direct computation

title: Proof
body_md: Since $q^2 \mid x$, Corollary~\ref{cor:separation} immediately gives that $q^2$ divides none of the other three quantities.
head: environment
name: Second proof (via strong separation

title: Remark
body_md: The first proof is self-contained and makes visible \emph{why} the residues $-1, -1, -7$ are harmless (they are too small in absolute value to be multiples of $q^2 \ge 25$, and nonzero). The second proof is shorter and generalizes better: it identifies the lemma as the special case ``$q^2$ hits the form $x$'' of the uniform statement that $q^2$ can hit at most one form, which applies symmetrically to fallback failures as well.
head: environment

label: prop:poly
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:poly}
If $p$ is a complete failure (Definition~\ref{def:completefailure}), then there exist four \emph{distinct} primes $q_1, q_2, q_3, q_4 \ge 5$ with
\[
q_1^2 \mid x, \qquad q_2^2 \mid 6x-1, \qquad q_3^2 \mid 2x-1, \qquad q_4^2 \mid 6x-7,
\]
and consequently
\[
(q_1 q_2 q_3 q_4)^2 \,\big|\, P(x), \qquad \text{where } P(x) = x(6x-1)(2x-1)(6x-7).
\]
Explicitly, $P(x) = 72x^4 - 132x^3 + 62x^2 - 7x$. The quartic $P$ has the four distinct rational roots $0, \tfrac16, \tfrac12, \tfrac76$; it is squarefree in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$, with discriminant $2^{14} \cdot 3^4 \cdot 7^2 = 65{,}028{,}096$. Moreover $(p-1)(p-2)(p-4)(p-8) = 18\,P(x)$.
head: environment
name: Polynomial reformulation

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:forms}, obstructions to each form come only from primes $q \ge 5$, so each non-squarefree form is divisible by $q_i^2$ for some prime $q_i \ge 5$. The $q_i$ are pairwise distinct by Corollary~\ref{cor:separation} (a single $q$ cannot square-divide two forms). Since the $q_i^2$ are powers of distinct primes each dividing a factor of the product $P(x)$, their product $(q_1q_2q_3q_4)^2$ divides $P(x)$. The expansion is a direct computation:
we have $(6x-1)(2x-1) = 12x^2 - 8x + 1$ and $x(6x-7) = 6x^2 - 7x$, whence $P(x) = (12x^2-8x+1)(6x^2-7x) = 72x^4 - 132x^3 + 62x^2 - 7x$; the roots of the factors are $0, \tfrac16, \tfrac12, \tfrac76$, which are distinct, so $P$ is squarefree over $\mathbb{Q}$. The discriminant evaluates to $72^6 \prod_{i<j}(r_i - r_j)^2 = 2^{14} \cdot 3^4 \cdot 7^2$. Finally $(p-1)(p-2)(p-4)(p-8) = 6x \cdot (6x-1) \cdot 3(2x-1) \cdot (6x-7) = 18 P(x)$.
head: environment

label: lem:ord
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ord}
For every prime $q \ge 5$, the multiplicative order of $2$ modulo $q^2$ is at least $20$, with equality if and only if $q = 5$.
head: environment
name: Order of $2$ modulo prime squares

title: Proof
head: environment

label: prop:extended
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:extended}
Let $A$ be any set of admissible exponents contained in an interval of length at most $19$. Then for every prime $q \ge 5$, the square $q^2$ divides at most one of the remainders $p - 2^a$, $a \in A$. In particular, $q^2$ divides at most one of the six quantities
\[
x, \qquad 6x - 1, \qquad 2x - 1, \qquad 6x - 7, \qquad 6x - 31, \qquad 2x - 21,
\]
corresponding via Lemma~\ref{lem:forms} to the admissible remainders $p - 2^a$, $a \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6\}$ (note $p - 64 = 3(2x - 21)$).
head: environment
name: Windowed separation

title: Proof
body_md: If $q^2 \mid p - 2^a$ and $q^2 \mid p - 2^b$ with $a < b$ in $A$, then $q^2$ divides the difference $2^b - 2^a = 2^a(2^{b-a} - 1)$, and since $q$ is odd, $q^2 \mid 2^{b-a} - 1$. Thus the order of $2$ modulo $q^2$ divides $b - a \le 19$, contradicting Lemma~\ref{lem:ord}. The six-form case follows since $\{0,1,2,3,5,6\}$ has width $6$, together with the normalizations $q^2 \mid p - 1$ if and only if $q^2 \mid x$, $q^2 \mid p-4$ if and only if $q^2 \mid 2x-1$, and $q^2 \mid p - 64$ if and only if $q^2 \mid 2x - 21$ for $q \ge 5$.
head: environment

label: rem:wieferich
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:wieferich}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:ord}, separation fails first when exponents exactly $20$ apart are compared, and then only at $q = 5$: both $p - 2^a$ and $p - 2^{a+20}$ can be divisible by $25$ (for $p$ in an appropriate class modulo $25$). This is the same threshold at which Hercher's heuristic computation \cite{hercher} changes character (his boundary case $2^{20}-1$), and the condition $q^2 \mid 2^d - 1$ is a Wieferich-type condition in the sense of \cite{gransound}.
head: environment
name: Wieferich-type boundary

label: lem:local
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Local densities at prime arguments

title: Proof
body_md: The condition $q^2 \mid f(x)$ determines $x$ modulo $q^2$ (the leading coefficient of each form is invertible modulo $q$), hence determines $p = 6x + 1$ in a single class modulo $6q^2$, and together with $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$, in a single class modulo $36q^2$ by CRT ($q \ge 5$ is coprime to $6$). This class is coprime to the modulus: $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$ is coprime to $36$, and $p \equiv 2^a \pmod{q^2}$ for the relevant $a \in \{0,1,2,3\}$ is coprime to $q$ since $q \ge 5 > 2$. Dirichlet's theorem gives density $1/\varphi(36q^2)$ among all primes, i.e., relative density $\varphi(36)/\varphi(36q^2) = 1/\varphi(q^2)$ within the class. Distinctness of the classes for distinct forms is a restatement of Corollary~\ref{cor:separation}: if two forms produced the same class modulo $36q^2$, any prime in it would have $q^2$ dividing two forms.
head: environment

label: thm:singleform
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:singleform}
Let $c \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}$. The set of primes $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$ for which $p - c$ is squarefree has relative density
\[
e_1 = \prod_{q \ge 5}\left(1 - \frac{1}{q(q-1)}\right) = 0.8974939526861\ldots
\]
within the class. The same holds with $c = 2^a$ for any fixed admissible exponent $a$.
head: environment
name: Single forms, unconditional

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\pi_c(N; m)$ for the number of primes $p \le N$ with $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$ and $p \equiv c \pmod{m}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:excluded}, no square of $2$ or $3$ divides $p - c$, so by inclusion--exclusion over square divisors,
\[
\#\{p \le N \text{ in the class} : p - c \text{ squarefree}\} \;=\; \sum_{d \le \sqrt{N}} \mu(d)\, \pi_c(N; d^2),
\]
and only $d$ coprime to $6$ contribute: for $2 \mid d$ or $3 \mid d$ the congruences $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$, $p \equiv c \pmod{d^2}$ are incompatible, so $\pi_c(N; d^2) = 0$. Set $y = (\log N)^{2}$ and split the sum. For $d \le y$ with $(d, 6) = 1$, the two congruences define a single admissible class modulo $36d^2$, and the Siegel--Walfisz theorem gives
\[
\pi_c(N; d^2) = \frac{\pi(N)}{\varphi(36)\,\varphi(d^2)} + O\!\left(N \exp(-c_0\sqrt{\log N})\right)
\]
uniformly. For $d > y$ we use the trivial bound $\pi_c(N; d^2) \le N/(36d^2) + 1$, so that range contributes $O(N/y + \sqrt{N})$. Since $\sum_{(d,6)=1} \mu(d)/\varphi(d^2) = \prod_{q \ge 5}(1 - 1/\varphi(q^2))$ converges absolutely (as $\varphi(d^2) = d\varphi(d) \gg d^2/\log\log d$), with tail $O(1/y)$, we obtain
\[
\#\{p \le N \text{ in the class} : p - c \text{ squarefree}\} = \frac{\pi(N)}{12} \prod_{q \ge 5}\left(1 - \frac{1}{q(q-1)}\right) + o(\pi(N)),
\]
and dividing by $\pi(N; 36, 7) \sim \pi(N)/12$ gives the theorem. The argument uses nothing about $c$ beyond admissibility, so it applies to any fixed admissible $2^a$.
head: environment

label: lem:lattice
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:lattice}
For squarefree $L$, the number of quadruples $(d_1, d_2, d_3, d_4)$ of squarefree positive integers with $\operatorname{lcm}(d_1,\dots,d_4) = L$ is $15^{\omega(L)}$, and
\[
\sum_{L \ge 1} \frac{15^{\omega(L)}}{L^{3/2}} < \infty .
\]
Consequently $\sum_{L > y} 15^{\omega(L)} L^{-2} \ll y^{-1/2}$ and $\sum_{L \le Z} 15^{\omega(L)} \ll Z^{3/2}$.
head: environment
name: Lattice sums

title: Proof
body_md: A squarefree quadruple with lcm $L$ assigns to each prime $q \mid L$ the nonempty subset of indices $i$ with $q \mid d_i$: there are $2^4 - 1 = 15$ choices per prime. Since $15^{\omega}$ is multiplicative, $\sum_L 15^{\omega(L)} L^{-3/2} = \prod_q (1 + 15 q^{-3/2}) < \infty$. The tail bound follows from Rankin's trick, $\sum_{L>y} 15^{\omega}L^{-2} \le y^{-1/2} \sum_L 15^{\omega} L^{-3/2}$, and the count from $\sum_{L \le Z} 15^{\omega(L)} \le Z^{3/2} \sum_L 15^{\omega} L^{-3/2}$.
head: environment

label: lem:moments
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:moments}
Uniformly in the shift $c \in \{1,2,4,8\}$ and $2 \le y \le N$,
\[
\textup{(i)} \ \sum_{8 < n \le N} D_c(n)^4 \ll N,
\qquad
\textup{(ii)} \ \sum_{8 < n \le N} D_c^{>y}(n)^4 \ll \frac{N}{\sqrt{y}} + N^{3/4}.
\]
head: environment
name: Fourth moments

title: Proof
body_md:
Expanding the fourth power and writing $L = \operatorname{lcm}(d_1, \dots, d_4)$,
\[
\sum_{8 < n \le N} D_c(n)^4 = \sum_{d_1, \dots, d_4} \#\{8 < n \le N : L^2 \mid n - c\}
\le \sum_{L} 15^{\omega(L)} \left(\frac{N}{L^2} + 1\right),
\]
where the sum may be restricted to $L^2 \le N$ (for $L^2 > N$ and $n > c$ the inner count is zero). By Lemma~\ref{lem:lattice} the $N/L^2$ part is $\ll N$ and the $+1$ part is $\sum_{L \le \sqrt{N}} 15^{\omega(L)} \ll N^{3/4}$, proving (i). For (ii) the quadruples satisfy $\min_i d_i > y$, hence $L > y$: the $N/L^2$ part is $\ll N \sum_{L > y} 15^{\omega(L)} L^{-2} \ll N/\sqrt{y}$, and the $+1$ part is again $\ll N^{3/4}$.
head: environment

label: thm:sf
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:sf}
For each subset $T$ of the four forms $\{x,\, 6x-1,\, 2x-1,\, 6x-7\}$, the set of primes $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$ for which \emph{all} forms in $T$ are squarefree has relative density
\[
\delta(T) = \prod_{q \ge 5} \left(1 - \frac{|T|}{q(q-1)}\right).
\]
head: environment
name: Squarefree equidistribution for several forms

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $t = |T|$ and let $c_1 < \dots < c_t$ be the corresponding shifts (a subset of $\{1,2,4,8\}$; recall that $q^2 \mid f(x_p)$ if and only if $q^2 \mid p - c_f$ for $q \ge 5$, and no square of $2$ or $3$ divides any $p - c_i$, by Lemmas~\ref{lem:forms} and~\ref{lem:excluded}). Set $y = (\log N)^{16}$ and, for each $i$, split the squarefree indicator into a truncated M\"obius sum and a tail:
\[
\mathbf{1}[\,p - c_i \text{ squarefree}\,] = M_i(p) + R_i(p),
\qquad
M_i(p) = \sum_{\substack{d \le y \\ d^2 \mid p - c_i}} \mu(d),
\quad
R_i(p) = \sum_{\substack{d > y \\ d^2 \mid p - c_i}} \mu(d),
\]
with the pointwise bounds $|M_i| \le D_{c_i}$ and $|R_i| \le D_{c_i}^{>y}$. Summing the product over primes $p \le N$ of the class gives $S(N) = \mathcal{M} + \mathcal{E}$, where $\mathcal{M} = \sum_p \prod_i M_i(p)$ and $\mathcal{E}$ collects the $2^t - 1$ cross terms, each containing at least one tail factor.

\emph{Main term.} Expanding each $M_i$ produces a sum over tuples $(d_1, \dots, d_t)$ with all $d_i \le y$ of $\mu(d_1)\cdots\mu(d_t)$ times the number of primes $p \le N$ with $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$ and $p \equiv c_i \pmod{d_i^2}$ for all $i$. Tuples in which some $d_i$ shares a factor with $6$ contribute nothing (the congruence is incompatible with the class, as in Theorem~\ref{thm:singleform}). Tuples with $\gcd(d_i, d_j) > 1$ for some $i \ne j$ also contribute nothing: a prime $q \mid \gcd(d_i, d_j)$ would give $q^2 \mid p - c_i$ and $q^2 \mid p - c_j$, hence $q^2 \mid c_j - c_i$ with $0 < |c_j - c_i| \le 7 < 25 \le q^2$, which is impossible --- the elementary heart of Corollary~\ref{cor:separation}, and note that no special case is needed at $q = 7$, since the conditions sit on the shifted primes directly. For the surviving tuples --- pairwise coprime and coprime to $6$ --- the CRT merges the conditions into a single class modulo $m = 36\prod_i d_i^2$, admissible because each $c_i$ is a power of $2$ and each $d_i$ is odd. Since $m \le 36y^8$ is a fixed power of $\log N$, Siegel--Walfisz applies uniformly, and with at most $y^t$ tuples the accumulated error is $o(N/\log N)$. The completed coefficient sum factors as an Euler product --- at each prime $q \ge 5$, either $q$ divides no $d_i$ or exactly one --- giving
\[
\sum_{\substack{d_1, \dots, d_t \text{ pairwise coprime} \\ (d_i, 6) = 1}} \frac{\mu(d_1)\cdots\mu(d_t)}{\prod_i \varphi(d_i^2)}
= \prod_{q \ge 5}\left(1 - \frac{t}{q(q-1)}\right) = \delta(T),
\]
absolutely convergent, with truncation error $O(y^{-1/2})$. Hence $\mathcal{M} = \delta(T)\, \pi(N; 36, 7) + o(N/\log N)$.

\emph{Cross terms.} A cross term has the shape $\sum_p Z_1 \cdots Z_t$ with each $Z_i \in \{M_i, R_i\}$ and $Z_{i_0} = R_{i_0}$ for some $i_0$. Bounding $|M_i| \le D_{c_i}$, $|R_{i_0}| \le D_{c_{i_0}}^{>y}$, dropping the primality of $p$, padding the product to four factors by the constant function $1$, and applying H\"older with exponents $(4,4,4,4)$:
\begin{multline*}
\left| \sum_p Z_1 \cdots Z_t \right|
\le \left(\sum_{8 < n \le N} D_{c_{i_0}}^{>y}(n)^4\right)^{\!1/4}
\left(\prod_{i \ne i_0} \left(\sum_{8 < n \le N} D_{c_i}(n)^4\right)^{\!1/4}\right) N^{(4-t)/4}\\
\ll \left(\frac{N}{\sqrt y} + N^{3/4}\right)^{\!1/4} N^{3/4}
\end{multline*}
by Lemma~\ref{lem:moments}, which is $\ll N/y^{1/8} + N^{15/16} = N/(\log N)^2 + N^{15/16} = o(N/\log N)$. The theorem follows.
head: environment

label: rem:sfscope
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:sfscope}
Nothing in the proof used $t \le 4$ beyond the padding in H\"older and the constant $15 = 2^4 - 1$: with $r$-th moments and $(2^r - 1)^{\omega}$, the identical argument covers any \emph{fixed} set of admissible exponents whose pairwise gaps are less than $20$, since the vanishing of non-coprime tuples then follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:ord} exactly as in Proposition~\ref{prop:extended}. In particular the five-form density $\rho_5$ used in Table~\ref{tab:exponents} is unconditional, as is $\rho_r$ for the first $r$ admissible exponents for every $r \le 16$ (the sixteenth admissible exponent is $a = 18$, so the window has width $18 < 20$). Beyond width $20$ the forbidden classes begin to coincide --- $2^{a+20} \equiv 2^a \pmod{25}$ --- and the local factors involve the number of distinct powers of $2$ modulo $q^2$, governed by $\operatorname{ord}_{q^2}(2)$; this is the Wieferich-type territory of \cite{gransound}, and we do not pursue it here.
head: environment
name: Scope: larger windows

label: thm:conditional
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:conditional}
The set of primes $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$ that admit a representation $p = 2^a + m$ with $m$ squarefree and $a \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ has relative density $1 - \rho_4$, where
\[
\rho_4 \;=\; \sum_{j=0}^{4} (-1)^j \binom{4}{j} e_j \;=\; 1.8637317202 \times 10^{-5} \;+\; O(10^{-14}).
\]
More generally, the set of primes for which the first $r$ admissible remainders all fail ($1 \le r \le 4$) has relative density $\rho_r = \sum_{j=0}^{r} (-1)^j \binom{r}{j} e_j$, with
\[
\rho_1 = 0.1025060473139\dots, \quad
\rho_2 = 0.0076726135528\dots, \quad
\rho_3 = 0.0004285664043\dots
\]
head: environment
name: Main density theorem

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:forms}, $p$ admits a representation with $a \le 3$ if and only if at least one of the four forms is squarefree at $x_p$. By inclusion--exclusion over subsets $T$ of the forms,
\[
\text{density}(\text{at least one squarefree}) = \sum_{\emptyset \neq T} (-1)^{|T|-1} \delta(T)
= \sum_{j=1}^{4} (-1)^{j-1} \binom{4}{j} e_j ,
\]
using Theorem~\ref{thm:sf} and the fact that $\delta(T)$ depends only on $|T|$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:local}: the local factors are $1 - |T|/(q(q-1))$ for every $q \ge 5$ regardless of which forms lie in $T$, by distinctness of the forbidden classes). The complement has density $\rho_4 = \sum_{j=0}^4 (-1)^j \binom{4}{j} e_j$. The same computation with the first $r$ forms gives $\rho_r$.

A remark on the numerics is in order, since the alternating sum defining $\rho_4$ cancels terms of size $O(1)$ down to $2 \times 10^{-5}$ --- a loss of roughly five significant digits. The Euler products $e_j$ were therefore evaluated with $50$-digit working precision, as products over primes $q \le 10^6$ multiplied by tail corrections $\exp\bigl(\sum_{q > 10^6} \log(1 - j/(q(q-1)))\bigr)$ computed via prime zeta functions; the check $\prod_{q\ge5}(1 - q^{-2}) = 9/\pi^2$ reproduces $16$ digits. All digits displayed here and above are correct, and the stated error bound on $\rho_4$ is conservative.
head: environment

label: cor:infinitude
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:infinitude}
The number of complete failures $p \le N$ is asymptotic to $\rho_4 \cdot \pi(N; 36, 7)$ with $\rho_4 = 1.8637317202\times 10^{-5} > 0$. In particular there are infinitely many primes $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$ admitting no representation $p = 2^a + m$ with $m$ squarefree and $a \le 3$; the first eleven are listed in Table~\ref{tab:failures}.
head: environment
name: Infinitude of complete failures

title: Proof
body_md: Immediate from Theorem~\ref{thm:conditional}, since a complete failure is precisely a prime of the class admitting no such representation with $a \le 3$ (Definition~\ref{def:completefailure}), and $\pi(N; 36, 7) \to \infty$.
head: environment

label: rem:density
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:density}
Theorem~\ref{thm:conditional} asserts that the exceptional set is \emph{sparse}, not that it is empty, and the distinction is genuine: complete failures exist, the smallest being $p = 4{,}851{,}151$ (with $x = 808{,}525$ and obstructing squares $5^2 \mid x$, $409^2 \mid 6x-1$, $7^2 \mid 2x-1$, $53^2 \mid 6x-7$), and by Corollary~\ref{cor:infinitude} there are infinitely many. Section~\ref{sec:computation} exhibits all eleven below $10^8$.
head: environment
name: Density, not universality

label: thm:integer
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:integer}
For each subset $T$ of the four forms, the set of integers $x \equiv 1 \pmod 6$, $x \le X$, with all forms in $T$ squarefree has density (relative to such $x$) equal to $\prod_{q \ge 5}(1 - |T|/q^2)$. Consequently, the set of $x \equiv 1 \pmod 6$ at which all four forms are non-squarefree has density
\[
\rho_4^{\mathbb{Z}} = \sum_{j=0}^{4} (-1)^j \binom{4}{j}\, d_j = 1.2018874348 \times 10^{-5}, \qquad d_j := \prod_{q \ge 5}\left(1 - \frac{j}{q^2}\right),
\]
where
\[
d_1 = \tfrac{9}{\pi^2} = 0.9118906527810\ldots, \quad d_2 = 0.8296305401295\ldots,
\]
\[
d_3 = 0.7529218854349\ldots, \quad d_4 = 0.6814789309610\ldots
\]
head: environment
name: Integer arguments, unconditional

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $T$ and a parameter $z \ge 7$, and let $A_z(X)$ count $x \le X$, $x \equiv 1 \pmod 6$, such that no prime $q \in [5, z]$ has $q^2 \mid f(x)$ for some $f \in T$. For a single prime $q \ge 5$, the condition $q^2 \mid f(x)$ is a single residue class for $x$ modulo $q^2$ (the leading coefficient of each form is invertible modulo $q$), and by Corollary~\ref{cor:separation} the classes attached to distinct forms in $T$ are \emph{distinct} --- the only delicacy is $q = 7$, where $7$ may divide both $x$ and $6x - 7$, but squarefreeness concerns $49$, and the two forbidden classes $x \equiv 0$ and $x \equiv 42 \pmod{49}$ are distinct by the final clause of Theorem~\ref{thm:coprime}. Hence exactly $|T|$ classes modulo $q^2$ are forbidden at each $q \in [5, z]$, and by the Chinese Remainder Theorem,
\[
A_z(X) = \frac{X}{6} \prod_{5 \le q \le z} \left(1 - \frac{|T|}{q^2}\right) + O\!\left(\prod_{5 \le q \le z} q^2\right).
\]
The count $N_T(X)$ of $x$ with all forms in $T$ squarefree differs from $A_z(X)$ only by $x$ suffering an obstruction $q^2 \mid f(x)$ with $q > z$; since $f(x) \le 6X + O(1)$, there are at most
$\sum_{f \in T} \sum_{q > z} \left( X/q^2 + 1 \right) \ll X/z + \sqrt{X}$
such $x$. Choose $z = \tfrac14 \log X$: then the accumulated error above is $\prod_{5 \le q \le z} q^2 \le e^{2\vartheta(z)} \le X^{3/5}$ for large $X$ by Chebyshev's bound $\vartheta(z) \ll z$, while the tail contributes $O(X/\log X)$; hence $N_T(X) = \tfrac{X}{6}\prod_{q \ge 5}(1 - |T|/q^2) + o(X)$, which is the first claim. (The cutoff must not be taken larger: for $z$ of order $\log X$ with a large constant, the product $e^{2\vartheta(z)}$ would overwhelm the main term.) Inclusion--exclusion over $T$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:conditional} gives the second. The constants $d_j$ and $\rho_4^{\mathbb{Z}}$ were computed exactly as in Theorem~\ref{thm:conditional}, with $d_1 = 9/\pi^2$ recovered to $16$ digits as a check.
head: environment

label: rem:abcrole
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:abcrole}
Theorem~\ref{thm:integer} uses nothing beyond Corollary~\ref{cor:separation} and elementary sieving, even though $F_T = \prod_{f \in T} f$ has degree up to $4$: separation collapses the square-divisor problem for the quartic into independent \emph{linear} problems, where the tail $\sum_{q > z}(X/q^2 + 1)$ is trivial to control. There is no genuinely quartic behaviour, hence no range of large $q$ in which the elementary method fails. We note that separation is a convenience rather than a necessity here: for any product of distinct linear forms, all but finitely many $q$ have $q^2$ dividing at most one factor, so the same elementary argument applies after excluding the divisors of the pairwise resultants.
head: environment
name: Where $abc$ would enter

title: Remark
body_md: The two constants differ by more than 50\%: $\rho_4^{\mathbb{Z}} \approx 1.20 \times 10^{-5}$ versus $\rho_4 \approx 1.86 \times 10^{-5}$. Restricting to prime arguments makes complete failures \emph{more} likely, because the conditions $q^2 \mid p - 2^a$ concentrate on the reduced residue classes. The data of Section~\ref{sec:computation} decisively favor the prime-corrected constant. Both are far smaller than the naive independence estimate $(1 - e_1)^4 \approx 1.10 \times 10^{-4}$ (or $(1 - d_1)^4 \approx 6.03 \times 10^{-5}$ with $d_1 = \prod_{q \ge 5}(1 - q^{-2}) = 9/\pi^2$), which ignores the mutual exclusivity of Corollary~\ref{cor:separation}: a single small prime such as $q = 5$ can account for only one of the four failures, and this negative correlation suppresses the joint event by a factor of about six.
head: environment

label: rem:cofinite
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:cofinite}
Theorem~\ref{thm:sf} in the extended form of Remark~\ref{rem:sfscope} gives, for each \emph{fixed} $r \le 16$, the exact relative density $\rho_r$ of primes failing all of the first $r$ admissible remainders, unconditionally. Taking $r = 16$ (admissible exponents $a \in \{0,\dots,18\} \setminus \{4, 10, 16\}$, a window of width $18 < 20$) yields an unconditional bound on the exceptional set of Conjecture~\ref{conj:cofinite}: it has relative density at most
\[
\rho_{16} = \sum_{j=0}^{16} (-1)^j \binom{16}{j} e_j = 4.2809 \times 10^{-27}.
\]
The cancellation here is far more severe than in Theorem~\ref{thm:conditional}: the largest term is $\binom{16}{8}e_8 \approx 4.8 \times 10^{3}$ against an answer of order $10^{-27}$, so roughly thirty significant digits are lost. This value was computed with $60$-digit working precision, and it is stable both under an increase of the precision to $100$ digits and under an increase of the Euler-product truncation from $10^6$ to $2.5 \times 10^6$.

One would like to let $r$ grow and conclude that the exceptional set has relative density zero. We have not established this, but we do not think the obstruction is where Remark~\ref{rem:sfscope} might suggest. The restriction to windows of width less than $20$ there is an artefact of how the local factors were stated, not of the method: for an arbitrary finite set $A$ of admissible exponents, the conditions $q^2 \mid p - 2^a$ for $a \in A$ single out the residues $2^a \bmod q^2$, and two exponents give the same condition precisely when they agree modulo $\operatorname{ord}_{q^2}(2)$. Coincident conditions merge consistently under the Chinese Remainder Theorem rather than conflicting, so the argument of Theorem~\ref{thm:sf} goes through with local factor
\[
1 - \frac{\#\{\,2^a \bmod q^2 : a \in A\,\}}{\varphi(q^2)},
\]
which agrees with $1 - |A|/\varphi(q^2)$ for all but the finitely many $q$ with $\operatorname{ord}_{q^2}(2) \le \max A$. Writing $\rho_A$ for the resulting density of primes failing every $a \in A$, the exceptional set of Conjecture~\ref{conj:cofinite} has relative density at most $\rho_A$ for every such $A$, and density zero would follow from $\rho_A \to 0$ as $A$ exhausts the admissible exponents. We have not proved that limit. It is not merely a matter of bookkeeping: for a given $p$, the exponents $a$ that are obstructed by a fixed $q$ form a congruence class modulo $\operatorname{ord}_{q^2}(2)$, so $\rho_A \to 0$ amounts to the assertion that the admissible exponents admit no covering by such classes, a question of covering-system type. Even density zero would then be a very long way from finiteness --- the squares have density zero --- and finiteness would require counting bounds uniform in $|A|$, which we do not have. We therefore state cofiniteness as a conjecture.
head: environment
name: How far the density method reaches

label: thm:computational
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:computational}
Every prime $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$ with $p < 10^8$ can be written as $p = 2^a + m$ with $m$ squarefree and $a \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 5\}$. Exactly eleven such primes are complete failures (no admissible $a \le 3$ works); each of the eleven is resolved at $a = 5$, i.e., $p - 32 = 6x - 31$ is squarefree. The exponent $a = 4$ is never usable (Lemma~\ref{lem:excluded}).
head: environment
name: Computational verification

label: conj:class
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj:class}
Every prime $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$ can be written as $p = 2^a + m$ with $a \ge 0$, $a \not\equiv 4 \pmod 6$, and $m$ squarefree.
head: environment
name: One-power conjecture for the class

label: conj:cofinite
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj:cofinite}
All but finitely many primes $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$ can be written as $p = 2^a + m$ with $a \ge 0$ and $m$ squarefree.
head: environment
name: Cofiniteness

label: prop:unbounded
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:unbounded}
For every $L$, there exist infinitely many primes $p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$ such that $p - 2^a$ is non-squarefree for every $a \le L$. Consequently $\limsup_p a_{\min}(p) = \infty$, where $a_{\min}(p)$ is the smallest usable exponent.
head: environment
name: The required exponent is unbounded

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A = \{a \le L : a \not\equiv 4 \pmod 6\}$ be the admissible exponents up to $L$, and choose distinct primes $q_a \ge 5$, one for each $a \in A$. The congruences
\[
p \equiv 7 \pmod{36}, \qquad p \equiv 2^a \pmod{q_a^2} \quad (a \in A)
\]
have pairwise coprime moduli, and each is a class coprime to its modulus ($2^a$ is coprime to $q_a$). By CRT they determine a single admissible class modulo $36\prod_a q_a^2$, which by Dirichlet's theorem contains infinitely many primes. Discard the finitely many such primes with $p \le 2^L$, so that $p - 2^a$ is a positive integer for every $a \le L$; infinitely many remain. For each of these, $q_a^2 \mid p - 2^a$ for every admissible $a \le L$, while $9 \mid p - 2^a$ for the inadmissible $a$; hence no $a \le L$ is usable.
head: environment

label: lem:herchercorrected
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:herchercorrected}
For real $0 < x \le \tfrac{1}{25}$ and integer $2 \le k \le 20$,
\[
\left| \log(1 - kx) - k \log(1-x) - \binom{k}{2} \log(1 - x^2) \right| \;<\; 7637\, x^3,
\]
and the constant is sharp up to rounding: $\sup_{0 < x \le 1/25} |e(x)|/x^3 = 7636.79\ldots$, attained as $x \to \tfrac1{25}$ at $k = 20$.
head: environment
name: Corrected form

title: Proof
body_md:
Combining the three logarithm series (all convergent for $0 < x < 1/k$, hence on our domain, where also $kx \le \tfrac45$),
\[
-e(x) \;=\; \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{k^n - k}{n}\, x^n \;-\; \binom{k}{2} \sum_{m \ge 1} \frac{x^{2m}}{m}.
\]
The $n = 1$ term vanishes and the $n = 2$ term cancels against the $m = 1$ term, leaving
\[
-e(x) \;=\; \sum_{n \ge 3} c_n(k)\, x^n,
\qquad
c_n(k) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{k^n - k}{n}, & n \text{ odd},\\[2mm] \dfrac{k^n - k^2}{n}, & n \text{ even},\end{cases}
\]
since for even $n = 2m$ the two contributions merge into $\bigl(k^n - k - 2\binom{k}{2}\bigr)/n = (k^n - k^2)/n$. Every coefficient $c_n(k)$ is nonnegative for $k \ge 2$ and $n \ge 3$, and each is nondecreasing in $k$. Therefore $e(x) < 0$, and
\[
\frac{|e(x)|}{x^3} \;=\; \sum_{n \ge 3} c_n(k)\, x^{n-3}
\]
is a sum of nonnegative nondecreasing functions of $x$ on $(0, \tfrac1{25}]$, hence nondecreasing in $x$, and nondecreasing in $k$ as well. The supremum over $2 \le k \le 20$ and $0 < x \le \tfrac1{25}$ is thus the single value at $(k, x) = (20, \tfrac1{25})$:
\[
25^3 \left| \log\tfrac15 - 20 \log\tfrac{24}{25} - 190 \log\bigl(1 - \tfrac{1}{625}\bigr) \right| \;=\; 7636.7967\ldots \;<\; 7637. \qedhere
\]
